opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I know it sounds counterintuitive. People hear "simulation company" and assume the first thing you build is the simulator, the physics engine, the renderer. But I think that's exactly the trap.

The simulator is a tool. The real question is: what problem are you trying to solve for robot learning? If you start by building a simulator, you end up optimizing for what simulators are traditionally good at, like nicer graphics, faster rigid-body physics, more realistic lighting. Those things matter, but they're not necessarily what limits embodied intelligence today.

What limits it is data. Specifically, data that actually transfers to the real world and actually makes a policy better. So I'd rather start from the other end. First, what tasks do we care about? What does the robot need to learn? Then, what data distribution do we need: which objects, which scenes, which interactions, how much variation? Then, how do we generate that data at scale, how do we label it, how do we evaluate whether a policy trained on it works on a real robot? Only once that whole pipeline is clear do you know what the simulator has to be good at, and what it can afford to be bad at.

If you build the simulator first, you make many expensive decisions before you have any feedback. You might spend two years making cloth simulation perfect when the bottleneck was asset diversity, or contact-rich manipulation, or simply the cost of building scenes. And simulators are huge engineering projects. Once you've committed to an architecture, it's very hard to change.

So in practice we tried to work backwards. Use existing tools where we can, even if they're imperfect, and get the data loop running end to end: generate, train, deploy on real hardware, measure the gap. That loop tells you where simulation fidelity actually matters. Then the simulator you build at the end is shaped by real requirements, not by imagination.

Another way to say it: the simulator isn't the product. The product is robot capability, and the simulator should be whatever is left over once you understand what that capability needs.

r002.rationale: It says simulator projects involve costly decisions and can be hard to change, but does not state that historically slow iteration kept value from reaching the simulator layer.

r003.rationale: It names data as the main bottleneck and mentions asset diversity and scene-building costs as examples, but does not identify insufficient high-quality assets and scenes as the primary reason simulation has not succeeded.

r004.rationale: It recommends establishing the data, training, deployment, and evaluation loop before building a simulator, but does not argue that simulation frameworks and APIs should come first.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the simulator is the part everyone wants to build first, and that's exactly why it goes wrong.

When I started out, the instinct was obvious: embodied intelligence needs data, real-world data is expensive and dangerous to collect, so let's build a beautiful physics engine with great rendering and generate infinite data. That sounds like the whole business. But a simulator by itself is just a very expensive toy. It has no definition of "good enough." You can always make the contact dynamics more accurate, the lighting more realistic, the friction model more detailed, and you never know when to stop, because nothing downstream is telling you which errors actually matter.

So what I'd argue is that you have to work backwards. First, what is the robot actually going to do? A warehouse picking task cares about grasp stability and clutter. A humanoid walking on uneven ground cares about contact timing and ground compliance, and barely cares about textures. Those two tasks want almost opposite simulators. If you build the engine before you've chosen the task, you build for everything and end up good at nothing.

Second, the thing that actually determines whether the sim is useful is the gap between sim and real. That gap is measured by a policy that trained in simulation and then got deployed. So before the simulator you need a real robot, a real task, and an evaluation loop. You collect some real data, you build the cheapest possible simulation, you train, you deploy, you see where it breaks. Maybe the robot slips because your friction was off. Fine, now you know precisely which part of the simulator to invest in. The failure cases become your roadmap.

Third, and this is more of a business point: a company that starts with the simulator ends up selling a simulator, and the market for general-purpose simulators is small and brutal. Nvidia and the game engines already sit there. A company that starts with the task ends up selling a capability, and the simulator becomes an internal asset that is tuned to exactly the places where the real world hurt you. That's much harder for anyone else to copy, because they'd have to repeat all of your failures.

So "build the simulator last" doesn't mean the simulator doesn't matter. It means you earn the right to build it by first understanding, from real deployment, what it has to be good at. Otherwise you spend two years polishing something and only find out afterwards which half of it was wasted.

astra-6.text:
Because the simulator is a means to an end. The goal is to help an embodied system learn something that works in the real world. Before you build the simulator, you need to understand what the system needs to learn, where it fails, and which parts of reality actually matter for those failures.

I’d start with a concrete task and a real-world baseline. Then ask: what’s the bottleneck? Is it perception, contact dynamics, planning, or simply a lack of varied training examples? Those problems call for very different kinds of simulation. If you build a general-purpose simulator first, you can spend years making things look realistic without knowing whether that realism improves the robot’s performance.

So when I say build the simulator last, I mean establish the learning and evaluation loop first. Use existing tools to test whether simulated data or simulated interaction helps. Once you can measure that benefit, you know what you actually need to build—and where greater fidelity is worth the cost.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the simulator is a means, and the first thing you need to understand is what problem it has to solve. What task is the robot learning? Where does it fail in the real world? What data or feedback would help it improve? Until you have those answers, you don’t really know what you need to simulate.

I’d start with a real task, collect data, train a model, and test it on the robot. That gives you a concrete picture of the gap. Maybe contact dynamics matter. Maybe visual variation matters more. Maybe the bottleneck is actually how you define success. Those lead to very different simulation requirements.

If you build the simulator first, you can spend years making a beautiful, general-purpose world without knowing whether it improves the robot. So building it last means letting the learning loop define the requirements. Build the simulation capability that addresses a demonstrated failure, then measure whether it transfers back to reality.
